marks: Mani, born near Ctesiphon in 216, began to preach his religion around 240.
Mani died in prison here under Bahram I (around 274–277).
Letters and books of a Manichaean community of the 4th century were found in this oasis village in Egypt.
Augustine was a Manichaean Hearer for nine years (373–382), at Carthage and Thagaste.
The capital of the Uyghur Khaganate, whose ruler Bögü Qaghan adopted Manichaeism in 762–763.
Manichaean books and paintings of the Uyghur kingdom were found in its ruins.
The image of Mani as the Buddha of Light, carved in 1339 in the last known Manichaean temple, near Quanzhou.
notes: Mani, born near Ctesiphon in 216, preaches a religion of the struggle between light and darkness and sends missionaries east and west; Shapur I tolerates him.
Diocletian orders the persecution of the Manichaeans (around 302), yet communities flourish in Egypt and North Africa, where the young Augustine is a Hearer (373–382).
Christian emperors and Sasanian kings persecute the Manichaeans; in the West they fade, while Sogdian merchants carry the faith east.
Manichaeans survive in Mesopotamia and Central Asia, where the eastern church forms a branch of its own, the Denawars.
A Manichaean teacher reaches the Tang court (694).
The Uyghur ruler Bögü Qaghan adopts Manichaeism (762–763), the faith of his empire for decades.
The Tang emperor Wuzong bans Manichaeism (843) after the fall of the Uyghur Khaganate (840); the Uyghurs of Turfan keep the faith.
Manichaeism is the court religion of the Uyghur kingdom of Qocho; the head of the church moves from Babylonia to Samarkand.
Buddhism wins the Uyghurs of Turfan; in southern China, Manichaeans live on as the 'religion of light' (Mingjiao) in Fujian.
The image of Mani as the Buddha of Light is carved at Cao'an near Quanzhou (1339).
The last Manichaean communities, in Fujian, fade after the 16th century.
